title: Audit Costs: 4 Extra Fees Compliance Teams Should Price in RFPs
summary: Learn what drives security audit costs, how SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI, and HIPAA affect pricing, and which RFP and SOW terms help compare bids and limit extras.
body_markdown:
Most organizations should expect to pay anywhere from a modest amount for a narrow, single-product readiness check to a substantially higher sum for a multi-location enterprise engagement with recurring testing requirements. Scope and depth of assessment drive that spread more than any other factor. The exact audit type and how ready your evidence is on day one will decide where your program actually lands inside that range.


---


> **TL;DR:**
>
>
> - Quotes rise with systems, control families, environments, and locations; ask vendors to separate sampling, specialist testing, travel, and change orders from the base fee.
> - Use fixed fees only for defined scopes; when requirements may shift, choose time and materials or phased pricing, with sample sizes and change orders specified.
> - Mandatory frameworks set minimum scope: PCI testing and scans recur, while ISO 27001 surveillance adds later costs; voluntary reviews can reduce scope to manage fees.
> - Keep system inventories, policies, and evidence current and centralized, then reuse prior assessment evidence where allowed to reduce duplicate evidence gathering during fieldwork.
> - Budget separately for internal staff time, remediation, and certification fees; the latter sit outside the auditor quote and may recur at surveillance intervals.

## 1. Typical cost ranges across small, mid-market, and enterprise engagements


Vendor quotes vary widely, but the pattern is consistent: price scales with the number of systems in scope, the control families being tested, and how many environments and locations an auditor has to touch. A small startup with one product and a handful of cloud services sits at the low end. A mid-market company running several products across multiple environments sits in the middle. A regulated enterprise with multiple business units, data centers, and third-party integrations sits at the top.


Standard vendor fees typically cover four phases: planning and scoping, fieldwork (interviews, control testing, evidence review), reporting, and project management to keep the engagement on schedule. Those four phases make up the baseline quote you will see in most proposals.


Beyond the baseline, a few add-ons regularly push the final invoice higher:


- Penetration testing or specialized technical assessments billed separately from the core audit
- Extended sampling when the auditor needs more evidence to support a conclusion
- Delays caused by evidence that was not ready when fieldwork started, which can extend billable hours
- Travel and onsite time for auditors visiting physical locations or data centers


A proposal that looks cheap on the cover page can grow fast once these line-items get added mid-engagement, so it helps to ask vendors to itemize them before you sign.


## 2. What actually moves the price: the primary cost drivers


Four or five variables explain most of the difference between a lean quote and an expensive one, and understanding them lets you estimate impact before a vendor even sends a proposal.


- **Scope breadth** : the number of systems, control families, environments, and physical locations in scope multiplies hours directly.
- **Audit type and rigor** : an attestation engagement with formal sampling requirements costs more than an advisory review of the same environment.
- **Evidence readiness** : when policies, inventories, and artifacts are scattered or outdated, auditors spend more hours chasing documentation instead of testing controls.
- **Third-party testing** : penetration testing, cloud-specific reviews, or privacy assessments are usually billed at specialist rates on top of the core engagement.
- **Schedule and travel** : compressed timelines and onsite requirements add rush fees and travel expense lines.


[NIST SP 800-53A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53Ar5.pdf) frames control assessments as information-gathering activities whose cost depends on how organizations tailor depth and coverage to risk, which is exactly why two companies of similar size can receive very different quotes for what looks like the same audit.


**Pro Tip:** *Ask every bidder to quote sample sizes and testing methods separately from the base fee. It is the fastest way to compare bids apples to apples.*


## 3. How to structure an RFP and SOW so bids are comparable


A well-built procurement document does more than invite pricing. It forces vendors to quote against the same scope, which is the only way to compare bids fairly.


1. **Pick a pricing model up front** : fixed-fee for well-defined scopes, time-and-materials when scope is still forming, or a phased structure that separates readiness, the audit itself, and remediation verification.
2. **Specify scope and sample sizes in the SOW** : list systems, control families, locations, and the sampling approach so vendors are not guessing.
3. **Require a documented change-order process** : this prevents scope creep from turning into surprise invoices mid-engagement.
4. **Set a realistic timeline** : most engagements of meaningful scope run several weeks to a few months, and compressing that window usually adds a rush premium.
5. **Clarify contract terms** : how travel and expenses are billed, what acceptance criteria apply to deliverables, and whether remediation support is included or billed separately.


The[GAO Cybersecurity Program Audit Guide](https://www.gao.gov/assets/870/862242.pdf) notes that audit objectives vary and that prioritizing tests based on risk, rather than attempting to assess every control, keeps engagements aligned with Yellow Book standards while controlling cost. Vendor[statements of work](https://www.verizon.com/business/service_guide/reg/Professional-Services-Security-Program-Assessment-ISO-27001.27002-SOW.pdf) commonly spell out project management, roadmaps, and travel billing as standard line-items, so look for those terms explicitly before you sign.


## 4. Audit type changes the price: SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI, and HIPAA


The compliance framework you are pursuing sets a floor on scope, and that floor shapes price more than almost any negotiation tactic.


- **SOC 2** : cost tracks the number of trust service categories in scope, the number of systems covered, and ongoing monitoring requirements, all of which increase sampling and labor hours.
- **ISO 27001** : initial certification audits require significant auditor time for scope definition and evidence review, and surveillance audits in later years add recurring cost even though they are typically lighter than the initial certification.
- **PCI** : required testing and mandated scan frequency add fixed, recurring costs that do not disappear once initial certification is achieved.
- **HIPAA** : regulation sets mandatory scope floors for covered entities and business associates, meaning the minimum coverage required by the rule itself puts a lower bound on price regardless of how lean an organization wants to be.


Mandatory, regulation-driven audits set a cost floor because scope is not something you can negotiate away.[Legal analysis of mandatory cybersecurity audit requirements](https://www.troutman.com/insights/ccpa-mandatory-cybersecurity-audits-are-coming/) draws this distinction clearly: voluntary assurance work can flex scope to manage cost, but mandatory audits cannot. If SOC 2 is on your roadmap, our[guide to SOC 2 compliance cost factors](https://www.skypher.co/post/soc-2-compliance-cost-factors-en) breaks down the specific drivers tech companies run into, and our[HIPAA assessment overview](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/hipaa-assessments-compliance-risk) covers the scope requirements that shape pricing for healthcare-adjacent organizations.


## 5. Practical ways to shrink audit cost without cutting corners


The fastest way to lower an audit bill is to reduce the hours an auditor spends chasing information instead of testing controls. That starts with readiness: maintain current system inventories, centralize policies in one place, and keep evidence artifacts versioned so nothing has to be reconstructed under time pressure.


A second lever is reuse.[NIST's RMF assessment-cases guidance](https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/risk-management/about-rmf/assess-step/assessment-cases-overview) describes how assessment cases can be adapted in depth and coverage to maximize common controls and reciprocity, which means a prior assessment's evidence often applies directly to a new one instead of being collected twice.


- Keep system inventories, policy libraries, and evidence artifacts current and centralized before engaging a vendor.
- Reuse prior assessment evidence and common controls wherever the framework allows it.
- Use automation to prefill vendor and auditor questionnaires, parse supporting documents, and flag missing artifacts before fieldwork starts.
- Consider a phased scope where the framework permits it, while recognizing that mandatory audits carry a required floor you cannot shrink below.

## 6. Breaking down what you're actually paying for


A full audit invoice usually bundles four distinct cost components, and separating them helps you see where your budget is really going.


**Auditor fees** cover the vendor's professional time: planning, interviews, control testing, sampling, and the formal report. This is typically the largest single line-item and scales directly with scope and audit type.


**Internal resource costs** are easy to overlook but real: the hours your own security, IT, and compliance staff spend gathering evidence, answering auditor questions, and coordinating logistics. On a poorly prepared engagement, internal hours can rival the vendor's own fees.


**Remediation expenses** cover the work needed to close gaps the audit uncovers, whether that is patching systems, rewriting policies, or implementing new controls. These costs sit outside the audit fee itself but are a direct consequence of it, and they vary enormously depending on how mature your controls were going in.


**Certification fees** , where applicable (ISO 27001 certification bodies, PCI Qualified Security Assessor fees), are a separate charge from the assessment work and often recur annually or at surveillance intervals.


Budgeting for an audit means budgeting for all four, not just the number on the vendor's cover page.


## 7. Weighing cost against speed and defensibility


In our work helping security and compliance teams prepare for audits and respond to the questionnaires that follow them, the trade-off that matters most is not cost versus speed. It is scope versus defensibility. A cheaper audit built on a narrower scope only pays off if that scope actually matches what your regulators, customers, or partners expect to see. Before negotiating price, get clear on what "defensible" means for your specific audience, then build the budget around that floor rather than around the lowest bid.


> *— Gaspard*

## FAQ


### How long does a typical security compliance audit take?


Most engagements run several weeks to a few months depending on scope, with planning and fieldwork taking the bulk of that time. Compressing the timeline usually adds a rush premium, since vendors have to allocate more staff in parallel to hit a tighter deadline.


### Does automation replace the need for a human auditor?


No. Automation tools shift hours away from manual evidence collection and questionnaire answering toward higher-value work like interpreting findings and planning remediation, but attestation and certification still require a qualified auditor to test controls and issue a formal opinion.


### What additional costs come up after the main audit fee?


Beyond the core auditor fee, expect internal staff time for evidence gathering, remediation costs for any gaps found, and separate certification fees for frameworks like ISO 27001 or PCI. Specialized testing such as penetration testing is also commonly billed as a separate line-item rather than bundled into the base quote.


### Can reusing a prior assessment actually lower audit cost?


Yes. NIST's assessment-cases guidance describes how reusing common controls and prior evidence across assessments reduces duplicate work, which directly lowers the hours a new audit requires.


### What is the difference between fixed-fee and time-and-materials pricing?


Fixed-fee pricing quotes one total for a clearly defined scope, which works well once requirements are locked in. Time-and-materials pricing bills by actual hours worked, which fits engagements where scope may shift as the assessment progresses.
